note: Long-running issues the new council (sworn in November 3, 2026) will keep deciding. Votes come from District minutes; when no one is named, nobody was recorded as opposed. Decisions reported out of closed meetings have no individual votes on record.

issues.title: Under One Roof and the downtown encampment
issues.question: What's happening with the encampment behind Under One Roof and the promised temporary housing?
issues.summary: Under One Roof at 37871 Third Avenue is Squamish's only shelter, supportive housing and food bank building, run by Squamish Helping Hands. An encampment grew behind it, and in October 2026 the District closed that site for good after a fire. The Province picked Squamish for its HEART and HEARTH program, which is meant to bring fenced, staffed temporary housing with supports, but no site has been chosen yet.

steps.label: Province names Squamish a HEART and HEARTH community
steps.note: The Province picked Squamish for outreach teams and temporary housing.

steps.label: Council asks staff to find a site with BC Housing
steps.note: Council made the decision in a closed meeting on January 20 and announced it March 3.

steps.label: First site, Loggers Lane park, dropped
steps.note: The site at 37956 Loggers Lane (Xwu'nekw Park) failed due diligence and was removed.

steps.label: Encampment behind Under One Roof closed
steps.note: After a September 18 fire, the District said people cannot return to the Third Avenue and Main Street site.

steps.label: Choosing a site for temporary housing
steps.note: The District and BC Housing are still weighing sites. If the site is District land, council must approve a lease.

steps.label: Neighbours told and invited to meet the project team
steps.note: BC Housing says it will contact neighbours once a site is confirmed.

steps.label: Temporary housing opens
steps.note: BC Housing's estimate is winter 2027/28.

history.what: The District permanently closed the encampment site behind Under One Roof after a fire; some residents moved to Vancouver Street and Loggers Lane. This was a staff decision, not a council vote.
A fire with propane tank ignitions broke out at the encampment while people were being moved out for a cleanup. No one was hurt.
The District announced more downtown patrols and a new Director of Public Safety. Council did not vote on it.
BC Housing presented the HEART and HEARTH program to council at a council workshop (Committee of the Whole).
Council announced it had removed the Loggers Lane park (Xwu'nekw Park) site from consideration, a decision made in a closed meeting on June 9.
Council announced it had endorsed the HEART and HEARTH designation and told staff to find a site with BC Housing.
Council received a staff update on encampments.
Council adopted a property tax exemption for Squamish Helping Hands at Under One Roof.

issues.what_next: The new council will likely see a temporary housing site come forward, and approve a lease if it is District land; BC Housing has said it needs a site soon to meet a March 2027 funding deadline.

issues.title: Supportive housing at 39900 Government Road
issues.question: When will the Government Road supportive housing be built?
issues.summary: BC Housing plans a six-storey building with 65 studio homes and 24/7 support staff at 39900 Government Road near Centennial Way, run by Squamish Helping Hands, on land the District is leasing for 60 years. A second building with 85 to 100 affordable rentals by Housing Squamish is planned on the same site but has no funding yet. Unlike Under One Roof, it will have no drop-in services; only residents who pay rent live there.

steps.label: Project announced
steps.note: BC Housing wrote to neighbours and held information sessions in June 2025.

steps.label: Council backs project and waives fees
steps.note: Council endorsed the project in principle and waived frontage works and fees.

steps.label: Council approves 60-year land lease
steps.note: Council endorsed the lease to the Provincial Rental Housing Corporation.

steps.label: Development and building permits
steps.note: These are approved by staff, not council; rezoning is not needed.

steps.label: Construction starts
steps.note: BC Housing expects to start in summer 2027.

steps.label: Affordable rental building funded
steps.note: Funding for the second building is not confirmed and it has no timeline.

history.what: Council endorsed a 60-year lease of the south part of the site to the Provincial Rental Housing Corporation and received BC Housing's letter of commitment to neighbours.
Council gave $190,000 of federal Housing Accelerator Fund money toward site servicing for the supportive housing.
Council endorsed in principle a 60-year lease to Housing Squamish for the affordable rental building, if it can get full construction funding.
Council waived frontage works and permit fees for the project.
Council announced it had endorsed BC Housing's supportive housing project and a 60-year lease in principle, decided in a closed meeting on May 20.
Council endorsed in principle a 60-year lease to Housing Squamish for affordable housing on the site and its funding application.

issues.what_next: Council has given its main approvals; the next public milestone is construction starting, which BC Housing expects in summer 2027, while council may be asked again about funding for the affordable rental building.

issues.title: Brennan Park Recreation Centre expansion
issues.question: Is Brennan Park getting a new pool or second ice rink?
issues.summary: Brennan Park is Squamish's only pool and arena, and residents have asked for years for more ice, more pool space and more programs. Grant-funded renovations to the existing building are nearly done, but a real expansion has no money set aside. A staff task force is studying what to build, what it would cost and how to pay for it, with results due by about mid 2027.

steps.label: Study funded in the budget
steps.note: Council put $125,000 for 2026 into the 10-year plan for the upgrade study.

steps.label: Engagement plan endorsed
steps.note: Council endorsed the task force's plan and asked staff to look at a council committee to help.

steps.label: Working out what to build, what it costs and how to pay
steps.note: Started June 2026 and planned to take about 12 months.

steps.label: Council picks an option and funding plan
steps.note: Council decides through the 10-year financial plan.

steps.label: Phase 2: secure funding
steps.note: Could include reserves, grants, partners and borrowing; borrowing usually needs elector approval.

steps.label: Phase 3: design and build
steps.note: Only after funding is secured; no build date exists yet.

history.what: Council endorsed the Recreation Centre Task Force engagement plan and asked staff to report on a Committee of Council to help shape the recommendation.
Council included the Brennan Park upgrade study in the draft 2026 to 2035 plan, with $125,000 for 2026.
Council received an update on the Brennan Park ice arena.
$10.4 million in federal and provincial grants was announced for building envelope and energy upgrades at Brennan Park.
Council approved the construction contract for phase one renovations, funded mostly by an $11.7 million grant, and the $10.4 million grant application.

issues.what_next: The task force's options, costs and funding plan are expected around mid 2027, and the new council will then decide what to build and how to pay for it.

issues.title: Woodfibre LNG taxes and lawsuits
issues.question: What happens now that council rejected the Woodfibre LNG tax deal?
issues.summary: Woodfibre LNG is the District's biggest taxpayer. In 2025 council set a very high major industry tax rate, and the company went to court over its 2025 and 2026 taxes and filed a damages lawsuit. A 10-year deal that would have paid at least $142 million and ended the lawsuits was rejected 5 to 2 on September 22, 2026, so normal taxation continues and the court cases go ahead.

steps.label: Agreement in principle negotiated
steps.note: The District asked the public for comments on the 10-year deal.

steps.label: Council votes on the deal
steps.note: Council rejected it 5 to 2.

steps.label: Court cases continue
steps.note: With no deal, the District says it will defend the lawsuits over 2025 and 2026 taxes.

steps.label: 2027 tax rate set for major industry
steps.note: Council sets tax rates each spring; the 2026 rate bylaw was adopted May 5, 2026.

steps.label: Any new agreement
steps.note: A future council could negotiate another deal, but Woodfibre calls the rejected one its final offer.

history.what: Woodfibre's CEO said the rejected deal was the company's fair and final offer.
Council declined the 10-year deal (fixed payments plus a capped tax bill) that would have ended the lawsuits.
history.votes: Councillors Andersen and French opposed (they supported the deal)

history.what: Council adopted the 2026 tax rate bylaw. The District says Woodfibre paid $7.7 million in 2026 while still under construction.
Woodfibre filed a civil lawsuit against the District, the Mayor and councillors seeking damages for alleged misuse of municipal powers.
Woodfibre asked the B.C. Supreme Court to quash the 2025 tax rate bylaw.
Council adopted the 2025 tax rate bylaw, setting the major industry rate at $125 per $1,000 of assessed value.

issues.what_next: The new council sets the 2027 major industry tax rate next spring and decides whether to reopen talks with Woodfibre, while the lawsuits move through the courts.

issues.title: 2027 budget and property tax increase
issues.question: How much will property taxes go up in 2027?
issues.summary: Each year council adopts a 10-year financial plan that sets how much money it raises from property taxes. Taxes rose 12.8% in 2026. Staff's draft for 2027 starts at a 10.4% increase (about $342 for the average home) before any new items, driven mostly by costs already committed such as RCMP contracts, wages and reserves.

steps.label: Budget workshops start
steps.note: The outgoing council reviewed utility, general fund and capital pieces in fall 2026.

steps.label: Draft shows 10.4% starting increase
steps.note: Before items still awaiting council endorsement.

steps.label: Public input and budget information night
steps.note: Email budgetfeedback@squamish.ca; the November information night date is to be confirmed.

steps.label: New council deliberates
steps.note: The District says the proposed budget is discussed over about three months.

steps.label: Financial plan bylaw readings and adoption
steps.note: Last year's plan got three readings January 6 and was adopted January 13.

steps.label: Tax rate bylaw adopted
steps.note: Rates are set in the spring; in 2026 this was May 5.

history.what: Staff presented the draft 2027 general fund: a 10.4% starting increase, of which 6.6% is costs already committed.
Council adopted the spring amendment to the financial plan and the 2026 tax rate bylaw.
Council adopted the District's first 10-year financial plan, with a 12.8% increase in property tax revenue for 2026.
Council decided the Cheekeye debris barrier's yearly costs will be split half from a local area tax and half from general taxes.
Council adopted the 2025 tax rate bylaw.

issues.what_next: The new council inherits the draft and is expected to adopt the 2027 to 2036 financial plan in winter 2026/27 and set 2027 tax rates in spring 2027.

issues.title: Official Community Plan update and growth
issues.question: Is the town's growth plan being rewritten, and where will new homes go?
issues.summary: The Official Community Plan (OCP), or town plan, is the master plan for where and how Squamish grows; the current one was adopted in 2018. Council has been adding provincial housing rules and neighbourhood plans, most recently pre-zoning Garibaldi Estates for more homes. Staff's draft budget proposes a full town plan rewrite starting in 2027.

steps.label: Province's housing update added to the town plan
steps.note: Council adopted the interim housing needs amendment (Bylaw 3139).

steps.label: Garibaldi Estates zoned for more homes ahead of time
steps.note: Final adoption of the Garibaldi Estates zoning bylaws was on the October 6 agenda; the minutes confirming the result are not posted yet.

steps.label: Full town plan update funded in the 2027 budget
steps.note: Staff's draft 2027 to 2036 plan proposes $97,500 in 2027 and about $540,000 more in 2028 and 2029; the budget is not yet adopted.

steps.label: Public engagement on the new plan
steps.note: Not yet scheduled.

steps.label: Readings and public hearing
steps.note: A town plan bylaw needs readings and, usually, a public hearing.

history.what: Bylaws zoning Garibaldi Estates for more homes ahead of time were on the agenda for final adoption (minutes not yet posted).
Council gave first and second reading to a Steep Slopes change to the town plan and set a public hearing.
Council gave three readings to five bylaws zoning Garibaldi Estates for more homes ahead of time; the medium lot zone passed 5 to 2.
history.votes: Councillors Hamilton and Greenlaw opposed the medium lot zone

history.what: Council adopted the town plan change adding the provincially required interim housing needs report.
Council adopted the Garibaldi Estates Neighbourhood Plan.

issues.what_next: The new council decides in the 2027 budget whether to fund a full town plan rewrite starting in 2027, and will see the Newport Ridge neighbourhood plan and other growth proposals.

issues.title: Paid parking and downtown parking
issues.question: Is paid parking coming to downtown Squamish?
issues.summary: A 2023 study found downtown's core close to full at peak times and suggested paid parking. Council chose instead to test paid parking at Darrell Bay only, and locals pay too after council dropped the resident pass. The pilot runs to the end of 2026, and staff report back in early 2027 on whether to expand paid parking downtown.

steps.label: Downtown parking study
steps.note: Council received the study and asked for a phased plan including paid parking.

steps.label: Public survey
steps.note: Over 2,600 people responded.

steps.label: Darrell Bay pilot approved
steps.note: Council approved a pilot at Darrell Bay until the end of 2026.

steps.label: Pilot runs
steps.note: $3 an hour, up to $10 a day in peak months.

steps.label: Staff evaluation to council
steps.note: Due early 2027.

steps.label: Decision on downtown paid parking
steps.note: Possible next phases include downtown and other tourist spots.

history.what: Council approved the Darrell Bay paid parking pilot to the end of 2026, with an evaluation in early 2027.
In committee, council removed the resident pass from the pilot, so residents pay too.
history.votes: Mayor Hurford and Councillor Greenlaw opposed removing it

history.what: Council told staff to prioritize a paid parking pilot at tourism spots as early as summer 2025.
Council received the 2023 Downtown Parking Study and asked for a phased plan that includes on-street paid parking.

issues.what_next: Early in 2027 the new council gets the Darrell Bay evaluation and decides whether, and where, to expand paid parking, including downtown.

issues.title: Regional transit to Vancouver and Whistler
issues.question: Will there ever be a public bus from Squamish to Vancouver or Whistler?
issues.summary: Squamish has local BC Transit buses but no public bus to Vancouver or Whistler. A service has been studied since 2015 and 2017 but has stalled over who governs and pays for it. In September 2026 local governments, the Lil'wat and Squamish Nations and the Province signed a memorandum to keep working on governance, funding and a service model.

steps.label: Transit Future Plan and Regional Transit Study
steps.note: The study proposed six weekday round trips between Whistler, Squamish and Metro Vancouver.

steps.label: Memorandum with the Province signed
steps.note: Partners agreed to plan governance, funding and service together.

steps.label: Agree who governs and who pays
steps.note: A regional transit commission and a local fuel tax have been proposed but not adopted.

steps.label: Council approves Squamish's share
steps.note: Local governments must commit their share of costs.

steps.label: Service starts
steps.note: No date.

history.what: The Sea to Sky Regional Transit Committee, including Squamish, signed a memorandum with the Province to plan an interregional service.
Council appointed Mayor Hurford to the Sea to Sky Regional Transit Committee for 2026.
For local buses, council chose a future frequent transit route from downtown to Garibaldi Village via Brennan Park.
Council had the Mayor write to provincial ministers about the lack of provincial funding for transit expansion.

issues.what_next: The new council appoints its member to the regional transit committee and may be asked to commit Squamish's share of costs once a governance and funding model is proposed; no date is set.

issues.title: Dikes, flood protection and the Cheekeye barrier
issues.question: What is being done to protect Squamish from floods and debris flows?
issues.summary: Much of Squamish sits on a floodplain, so the District keeps raising dikes under its flood hazard plan, often with grants and some borrowing. A new $18 million sea dike at Xwu'nekw Park protects downtown, and a Squamish River dike was raised at Judd Slough. The District has also become responsible for the Cheekeye debris flow barrier north of Brackendale, whose upkeep is now in the tax plan.

steps.label: Integrated Flood Hazard Management Plan
steps.note: Council adopted the plan that sets which dikes to upgrade first.

steps.label: Downtown sea dike at Xwu'nekw Park
steps.note: All piling, including the sheet pile wall, was complete by March 2026; the District planned to finish in summer 2026.

steps.label: 2026 flood upgrade borrowing given three readings
steps.note: Loan Authorization Bylaw 3251 for annual flood upgrades.

steps.label: Elector approval for borrowing
steps.note: The District usually seeks approval for borrowing through an Alternative Approval Process.

steps.label: Bylaw adopted and next dike projects

history.what: Council gave three readings to borrowing bylaws for annual flood protection upgrades.
Council adopted a $2 million flood protection loan bylaw after an Alternative Approval Process, and carried $3.4 million left from the Judd Slough dike project forward to more dike work.
Council set Cheekeye barrier costs at half local area tax and half general tax in the financial plan.
Council adopted a new Floodplain Management Bylaw.
Council adopted the borrowing bylaw for the Xwu'nekw Park sea dike.
Council accepted responsibility as the local diking authority for the Cheekeye debris flow barrier.

issues.what_next: The new council is expected to adopt the 2026 flood upgrade borrowing once elector approval is complete, and fund the next dike projects and Cheekeye barrier upkeep in the 2027 budget.

issues.title: Woodfibre LNG worker floatels
issues.question: What's the status of the floating worker camps at Woodfibre LNG?
issues.summary: Woodfibre LNG houses most of its construction workers on 'floatels', ships moored at the plant site. Council controls the land use permit for them. Council refused a permit in April 2024 before the provincial Environmental Assessment Office ordered workers housed on the floatel, and in July 2025 council approved a two-year temporary use permit for two floatels.

steps.label: First permit refused
steps.note: Council defeated the one-year permit.

steps.label: New permit process
steps.note: Council told staff to seek land use compliance through a new permit.

steps.label: Two-year permit for two floatels approved
steps.note: With conditions including BC Hydro shore power for Floatel 2.

steps.label: Permit term runs
steps.note: The plant is expected to finish construction in 2027.

steps.label: Renewal or end of permit
steps.note: If floatels are still needed when the permit ends, council would have to decide on a renewal or a new permit.

history.what: Woodfibre's lawsuit against the District cites the 2024 floatel permit refusal as causing costly delays.
Council approved a two-year temporary use permit for Floatel 1 and Floatel 2.
Council announced it had directed staff to work with Woodfibre on a new permit.
Woodfibre withdrew its application after a provincial order to house workers on the floatel; the District said the order did not override its zoning.
On reconsideration, council referred the permit back to staff to negotiate tougher terms, including a $10 million security deposit.
Council defeated a one-year permit for the first floatel.
history.votes: Councillors Greenlaw, Pettingill, Stoner and Hamilton opposed the permit

issues.what_next: The new council may face a renewal request if the floatels are still needed when the two-year permit ends, roughly mid to late 2027.
